title: Molerats
summary: Molerats is a cluster name for activity that public reporting associates with a Gaza-based group and frames as politically motivated rather than financially driven, with targets in Israel, the Palestinian territories, and neighbouring Middle Eastern states. Reporting describes social engineering through email, social media, and messaging applications, including lures built around political and humanitarian news, fake personas used to build rapport, and delivery through archive files, short link services, and file-sharing platforms rather than mail attachments alone. Payloads have included commodity remote access families and, in some reported campaigns, destructive wiper components, which means the group has demonstrated both espionage and disruption intent. Attribution statements differ between vendors and are generally held with moderate confidence, so the label should be treated as an analytic cluster. Defenders see decoy documents, archive and shortcut files, script interpreters started by user action, and outbound sessions to newly registered or short-lived infrastructure.

beginner.definition: Molerats is a research name for a group that public reports link to Gaza. It uses politics and news as bait to trick people into opening harmful files. It is known for both spying and, in some cases, destroying data.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attacks that use real news events are hard to spot, because the topic feels urgent. The group also talks to targets directly on social media, which builds trust first. Some campaigns destroyed data instead of stealing it. That means the damage can be immediate and severe. Staff training and network monitoring are both important here, because the first contact is often human.
howItWorks: The attackers pick a news story that their targets already care about.
One of them builds a fake profile that looks like a friendly and helpful contact.
They spend weeks building trust with friendly messages and small offers of help.
The harmful file finally arrives inside an archive, a short link, or a sharing site.
Opening that file quietly starts a remote control program on the victim machine.
Some campaigns steal nothing at all, and instead erase files to cause disruption and fear.
beginner.example: Think of a stranger who joins a community group and spends weeks being helpful. He learns who trusts whom and which topics people argue about. He finally shares a document about a topic everyone follows. People open it at once, because they know his name. Later the group finds that the friendly member was never a member at all. Social engineering attacks work exactly like this. The relationship is the delivery method, and patience is what makes it effective.
takeaways: A believable story is often more dangerous than clever software.
Attackers may build trust for weeks before sending anything harmful.
Backups and tested recovery plans protect you when data is destroyed.

objectives: Explain how social engineering builds trust before any malicious payload is delivered.
Describe delivery channels that bypass mail attachment filtering, such as archives and sharing links.
Distinguish espionage intent from destructive intent and the response each requires.
Identify host evidence of archive and shortcut files starting script interpreters.
Explain why attribution in this region is reported with moderate confidence.
Describe backup and recovery controls that limit the impact of destructive campaigns.
